strengths: The paper targets an important and clearly NLP-relevant evaluation gap: realistic travel-planning agents need tool use, multi-turn preference elicitation, and infeasibility detection, which are not jointly covered well by prior benchmarks.

The benchmark design is usefully decomposed into single-turn, multi-turn, and unsolvable subsets, and the tool suite covers several practical travel domains such as maps, routes, flights, trains, weather, and web search.

The sandbox/cache idea is a sensible direction for making tool-augmented agent evaluation more stable than live API calls, and the paper reports results over several closed- and open-source models with repeated runs.
The comparison with prior travel-planning benchmarks and the analysis of tradeoffs between interactive planning and unsolvable detection help position the contribution.
weaknesses: The central reproducibility claim is not adequately supported. The paper does not specify whether the queries, user profiles, tool-call cache, judge prompts/rubrics, trajectories, sandbox code, or simulated cache-miss outputs will be released, and many construction details are missing.

The data construction pipeline relies heavily on LLMs without sufficient validation: solvability is decided by two models, multi-turn status is induced by GPT-4.1 assistant behavior, user replies are simulated by GPT-4.1, and final scoring is judged by GPT-5.1. There is no human audit, agreement analysis, or error analysis showing these labels and scores are reliable.

The sandbox still uses an LLM to generate responses for cache misses. This weakens the claim of deterministic, real-world tool evaluation unless the model, prompt, decoding, retrieved examples, and outputs are fixed and released; it may also introduce fabricated tool results.

The evaluation metric is under-justified. The multiplicative penalties for tool errors and meta-judge calibration can strongly affect scores, but there is no validation against human judgments, no sensitivity analysis, and no discussion of whether GPT-5.1 judging favors particular model styles.

There is a clear inconsistency in the reported overall score: Table 3 labels Overall as the average of penalty-adjusted multi-turn and single-turn scores, while Equation 9 and the numbers include the unsolved score as a third component.

The experimental comparison is thin for a benchmark paper. The paper does not evaluate prior travel-planning systems or solver/RAG baselines under the new benchmark, so it is hard to assess what capabilities the benchmark uniquely reveals beyond model ranking.

Claims about real-world coverage are only partially substantiated. The paper says queries come from real user questions but does not describe sources, sampling biases, privacy handling, geographic/language distribution, task-type counts, or examples of instances.

The unsolvable evaluation is likely prompt-sensitive: models are explicitly instructed to emit a special tag, and accuracy only checks whether the first response contains that tag, which may measure compliance with a benchmark convention rather than robust feasibility judgment.

strengths: The paper identifies a real gap in travel-planning evaluation: existing benchmarks under-cover multi-turn interaction, tool use across diverse travel domains, and unsolvable requests. These are relevant and timely capabilities for NLP agent evaluation.

The benchmark design has several promising ingredients, including separate single-turn, multi-turn, and unsolvable subsets; a travel-specific tool suite; cached tool outputs for stability; and reporting across both closed-source and open-source models.
The inclusion of an unsolvable subset is a useful direction, since feasibility recognition is often omitted from agent benchmarks despite being important in realistic user-facing planning tasks.
weaknesses: The central empirical support is not rigorous enough for acceptance. The dataset construction is described only at a high level: the source of the 'real user questions,' privacy/license considerations, annotation instructions, filtering criteria, examples, and release plan are all unclear. Without these details, the claimed realism and reproducibility are difficult to assess.

The multi-turn subset is not based on real multi-turn user interactions. Queries are labeled as multi-turn if a GPT-4.1 assistant asks follow-up questions in three simulated runs, with GPT-4.1 also simulating the user. This makes the benchmark heavily model-contingent and weakens the claim that it evaluates real dynamic user-agent interaction.

The evaluation protocol relies almost entirely on LLM-as-a-judge scoring and an additional LLM meta-judge, but the paper provides no human validation, judge agreement analysis, prompt details, calibration study, or robustness analysis. This is especially concerning because subjective plan quality is the main reported outcome.

The sandbox reproducibility claim is overstated. Cache misses are handled by retrieving similar calls and asking an LLM to synthesize tool responses, but the model, decoding settings, validation procedure, and factual fidelity of these simulated responses are not sufficiently specified. This can introduce uncontrolled artifacts into both task execution and scoring.

There is an internal inconsistency in the overall-score description: Table 3 says the overall score is the average of multi-turn and single-turn penalized scores, but the reported numbers match averaging those scores together with unsolved accuracy, as in Equation 9. This kind of inconsistency undermines confidence in the experimental reporting.

The experiments are thin for a benchmark paper. There is no comparison on shared instances against prior benchmarks, no ablation of the sandbox/cache-miss mechanism, no analysis of judge penalties versus actual task failures, no statistical uncertainty beyond averaging runs, and only limited qualitative error analysis.

The model set and claims are not well contextualized. The paper evaluates a small number of models and then concludes that the benchmark is challenging, but without stronger baselines, oracle/tool-valid upper bounds, human performance, or prior-system comparisons, the difficulty and diagnostic value remain under-supported.

Reproducibility is currently inadequate: prompts, user profiles, tool schemas, cache contents, simulator instructions, judge rubrics, and code availability are either missing or insufficiently specified. For a benchmark contribution, these are not peripheral details but part of the core contribution.

strengths: The paper targets an important and clearly NLP-relevant problem: evaluating tool-augmented LLM agents in realistic travel planning, including interaction, constraint handling, and infeasibility detection.

TravelBench improves over narrow fixed-itinerary benchmarks by including broader travel-query types, multi-turn dialogues, single-turn tasks, and an unsolvable subset, which are well motivated by real agent use cases.

The sandbox design with cached tool outputs is a valuable step toward stable evaluation, and the tool set covers several core travel-planning functions such as maps, routing, flights, trains, weather, and web search.

The experimental results are informative: they show that current models still struggle, that penalties substantially reduce scores, and that unsolvable detection and interactive planning appear to be distinct capabilities.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not yet fully convincing. The paper does not clearly specify whether the full queries, user profiles, tool-call cache, prompts, judge rubrics, simulator prompts, and cache-miss simulator are released; without these, the benchmark would be difficult to reproduce independently.

The dataset construction relies heavily on LLM decisions with little validation. Solvability labels, unsolvable categories, and single-turn versus multi-turn labels are assigned by models or GPT-4.1 trajectories, but there is no human agreement study or error analysis to establish label reliability.

The evaluation protocol is underjustified. GPT-5.1 is used as the judge and meta-judge while also being one of the evaluated systems, and there is no correlation with human judgments, inter-judge robustness test, or ablation of the meta-judge calibration factor.

The sandbox cache-miss mechanism weakens the claim of deterministic tool-grounded evaluation: when the cache misses, an LLM simulates tool responses from retrieved examples, which may introduce hallucinated or judge/model-dependent evidence unless carefully audited.

The paper has an internal inconsistency in reporting the overall score: the table caption says Overall is the average of the penalty-adjusted multi-turn and single-turn scores, but Equation 9 and the reported values include the unsolved score as well.

The empirical comparison is somewhat limited for a benchmark paper. There is no direct evaluation on prior benchmark instances, no ablation of multi-turn simulation or penalties, and little qualitative analysis of common failure modes beyond high-level observations.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely problem: evaluating tool-using LLM agents in realistic travel-planning scenarios beyond static itinerary generation.
TravelBench has a useful task decomposition into single-turn, multi-turn, and unsolvable queries, which targets distinct agent capabilities that prior travel benchmarks often conflate or omit.

The benchmark design includes a reasonably broad tool suite covering maps, routing, transportation, weather, and web search, and the paper provides detailed prompts, rubrics, examples, and tool definitions.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering many proprietary and open-source models, and the results reveal meaningful capability tradeoffs, especially between task completion and recognizing unsolvable requests.
The authors make a serious effort to validate dataset labels and judge reliability through human checks, repeated judge runs, offline/online comparisons, and framework-control experiments.
weaknesses: The central claim of fully real-world, reproducible tool evaluation is weakened by low exact cache-hit rates and reliance on an LLM-based tool simulator for cache misses; many returned tool outputs may therefore be synthetic rather than real API results.

Reproducibility remains uncertain: the extracted manuscript indicates public code/data but does not provide a visible link, and the benchmark depends on proprietary logs, production-grade tools, and closed or version-sensitive models for judging, simulation, and dataset construction.

The single-turn versus multi-turn split is defined by the behavior of GPT-5.1 and Gemini-3-Flash rather than by an independent task criterion, so the labels may partly encode the prompting and tendencies of those models.

The evaluation protocol relies heavily on LLM-as-a-judge scoring with only limited human validation: 100 GPT-5.1 multi-turn trajectories are checked, but there is less evidence for judge reliability across models, languages, task types, and lower-quality trajectories.

The unsolvable evaluation is quite narrow, reducing success to whether the first response contains a special tag, which may reward conservative abstention and may not capture nuanced boundary handling or partial assistance.

Some score construction choices are under-justified, including equal averaging across subtasks, multiplicative meta-judge calibration, and the tool-error penalty; these choices can materially affect model rankings.

The realism claims are geographically and linguistically constrained: the data appears to come from a Chinese online platform and China-focused travel tools, but the title and framing suggest broader real-world travel planning.

Privacy and ethics are discussed, but the use of real user preference logs and LLM-generated demographic attributes raises residual concerns about consent, representativeness, and whether synthetic profile fields distort the benchmark’s personalization claims.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and timely NLP problem: evaluating tool-using, multi-turn travel agents on realistic open-ended user requests rather than only synthetic itinerary-planning tasks.
The benchmark design usefully separates three practically important capabilities: completing fully specified requests, interacting to elicit missing preferences, and recognizing unsolvable requests.

The authors put substantial effort into infrastructure: ten travel-related tools, cached tool responses, a sandbox, tool-call error penalties, multiple evaluated model families, and repeated-run stability checks.
The paper includes prompts, examples, dataset statistics, human spot checks, and some offline/online comparison, which are helpful for understanding the intended evaluation pipeline.
weaknesses: The central claim of a 'truly real-world' and reproducible benchmark is not fully supported. The data source is only vaguely described as an online platform, the code/data link appears absent or redacted, and the release status of raw queries, profiles, cached tool calls, tool schemas, and evaluation traces is unclear.

The dataset construction is highly model-dependent. Unsolvability is labeled by agreement among LLMs, and the single-turn versus multi-turn split is determined by the behavior of two particular assistant models. This risks circularity: the benchmark categories may reflect model prompting artifacts rather than intrinsic task properties.

The user profiles mix real preferences with LLM-synthesized demographics and lifestyle attributes, yet the paper continues to frame the benchmark as grounded in real user preferences. This weakens the validity of personalization and implicit-preference claims.

The sandbox is less clearly faithful than advertised. Cache-hit rates are often low, especially for multi-turn settings, and misses are handled by embedding retrieval plus LLM-simulated tool responses. That means a significant part of the environment may be generated rather than real tool output, undercutting claims of stable real-world tool use.

The evaluation relies heavily on LLM-as-a-judge scoring and a meta-judge, both using proprietary or very recent models. The human validation is limited and not sufficiently detailed to establish reliability across domains, models, languages, and error types.

The unsolvable-task metric is too shallow: checking whether the first response contains a special tag does not robustly measure boundary recognition, calibrated refusal, or helpful recovery behavior. It may reward prompt compliance rather than genuine recognition of infeasibility.

The experimental analysis is mostly descriptive. The paper reports model rankings but provides limited ablations, limited comparison to prior benchmarks beyond a feature table, and little evidence that scores predict actual user satisfaction or downstream task success.

The scope is narrower than the framing suggests: the benchmark appears centered on China-specific travel data and tools, while the title and claims imply broader real-world travel planning. Generalizability to other regions, languages, tool ecosystems, and privacy regimes is not demonstrated.

Important ethical and reproducibility issues remain unresolved. The paper uses sensitive real user queries and inferred/synthesized profiles, but gives insufficient detail about consent, data governance, de-identification failure analysis, and what will actually be released.

Overall, this is a potentially useful benchmark paper, but the current submission overclaims relative to the evidence. I would not recommend main-conference acceptance; a Findings-level case is borderline and would require clearer release details, stronger human validation, less model-circular dataset labeling, and a more convincing account of sandbox fidelity.

strengths: Timely and practically relevant benchmark contribution for tool-using travel agents, going beyond itinerary generation to include POI search, routing, transport, weather, broad travel intents, multi-turn clarification, and unsolvable requests.

The dataset design is stronger than many prior travel-planning benchmarks: 1,100 instances from real user queries/preferences, explicit single-turn/multi-turn/unsolvable splits, 10 travel-related tools, and a large cached tool-response sandbox.

The paper gives useful validation rather than only presenting a benchmark: human checks of de-identification and split quality, agreement statistics for feasibility and turn labels, judge-human MAE comparisons, repeated-run stability, and offline-vs-online sandbox comparisons.

The experimental results are informative and show nontrivial capability differences across frontier and open-source models, especially the imbalance between task completion and recognizing unsolvable requests.
The paper is generally clear, well organized, and includes extensive appendices with tool definitions, prompts, examples, and additional baselines.
weaknesses: The strongest claims of being 'truly real-world' and reproducible are somewhat overextended. The raw data source, platform distribution, tool APIs, compliance constraints, and release details are not sufficiently transparent to know whether the community can fully reproduce or audit the benchmark.

The sandbox still depends heavily on LLM simulation for cache misses, with relatively low exact cache-hit rates in several settings. The offline-vs-online comparison is reassuring but limited to a few models and may not cover different tool-use behaviors or argument distributions.

The evaluation relies on LLM-as-a-judge and a meta-judge, both using proprietary or rapidly changing models. Human validation is useful but limited in scale and appears concentrated on sampled multi-turn trajectories, so evaluator bias and model-specific blind spots remain concerns.

The single-turn versus multi-turn split is partly defined by the behavior of specific models rather than an independent task property, which may bake current model tendencies into the benchmark labels.
The benchmark is geographically and linguistically concentrated in China and travel-platform-style usage; this is a valid scope, but it weakens broad claims about general real-world travel planning.

Some scoring choices are brittle or under-justified, such as unsolvable evaluation via first-response tag matching and multiplicative penalties for judge calibration and tool-call errors. These choices may affect model rankings beyond the underlying task quality.
